speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. Si. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: ORDERS IN COUNCIL GAZETTED AND TABLED
speechtext:
At the risk of making some of our newspaper friends believe that I am providing the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) with another easy victory, I should like to deal with a couple of questions that he has placed on the order paper, one of which was passed as an order for return.
The first question was as follows:
1.	How many orders In council relative to the provisions of the Immigration Act have been passed since the first day of July, 1947?
2.	Of said orders in council, how many have not been (a) published in the Canada Gazette; (b) tabled in parliament?
Answer: 121, of which ten were published in the Canada Gazette and none tabled in parliament.
The other question, passed as an order for return, read as follows:
1.	How many written permits provided for by section four of the Immigration Act were issued by the minister during each of the years 1947 and 1948 (a) authorizing any person to enter Canada; (b) authorizing any person to remain in Canada; and in either case without being subject to the provisions of the said act?
2.	How many of these permits have been included in a return laid before parliament within thirty days after the commencement of the next ensuing session of parliament in each of the said years?
Answer: 1. 1947-twenty-four authorizing persons to enter Canada and three authorizing persons already here to remain in Canada; 1948-twenty-five authorizing persons to enter Canada and twenty-six authorizing persons already here to remain in Canada.
2. All the above permits were included in the following returns: For 1947-January 28, 1948, Votes and Proceedings, page 94; for 1948 -January 27, 1949, Votes and Proceedings, page 16.
The answers to two other questions, which have also been passed as orders for return, will be tabled as soon as the necessary information has been collected.
I have had a careful check made of all the orders in council relative to the provisions

Immigration
of the Immigration Act, including those orders regarding the entry into Canada of individuals or groups of individuals during the period from July 1, 1947, to March 4, 1949.
As will be noted from one of the answers just given, there were 121 orders in council in all. Included in this total were eleven orders of general application amending the regulations. Of these, ten were published in the Canada Gazette; the eleventh-P.C. 4852 of November 26, 1947-merely repealed certain obsolete orders in council and its publication was therefore not considered necessary. Next there were sixteen orders in council dealing with unnamed groups of persons, such as the displaced persons, the Maltese, the Estonians, the movement of orphan children, and the like. Then there were nineteen orders in council of an administrative or executive character. Lastly there were seventy-five orders in council which waived the provisions of the general immigration regulations in regard to the persons named therein.
I now wish to table copies of all the orders in council included in the four groups to which I have referred. This in fact includes all orders in council relating to the Immigration Act that have been passed during the period July 1, 1947 to March 4, 1949. The tabling of these orders in council will also serve as a return to the motion on the order paper in the name of the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross).
I think I should take advantage of this occasion to say a word about the manner in which the government-not only this government but all preceding governments-have administered the question of exceptions under the regulations for the admission of immigrants.
Immigration into Canada is controlled by the terms of the Immigration Act and by the regulations made in accordance with those terms. The act does not define the classes or categories of persons who are admissible to Canada as immigrants. On the other hand it does define certain prohibited classes, including persons suffering from some forms of mental or physical ailment, criminals, advocates of the use of force or violence against organized governments, spies and certain others enumerated in the terms of the statute. Persons within these prohibited classes cannot be admitted to Canada as immigrants unless and until the Immigration Act is amended by parliament. On the other hand it is in the general orders in council that one finds in the definition of persons who are from time to time admissible.

The reason for such an arrangement is to provide a certain flexibility which would not be possible if every changing circumstance had to be met by an amendment to the act. Because the regulations made under the act can be altered by order in council, this provides the flexibility without which the whole administration of the Immigration Act would be so rigid as to be practically unworkable.
It is of course inevitable that in dealing with human beings, as is the case in the administration of the Immigration Act, special circumstances will arise in which it is proper to make exceptions to the general rules. This happens most frequently as a result of humanitarian considerations. For example, a person is found to be living in Canada who entered several years ago contrary to the regulations. In the meantime he has become well established, is married to a Canadian citizen, and has a family. In such circumstances, if the regulations had been embodied in the act, it would have been necessary to pass a special act of parliament to provide for the admission of that one person. Under the procedure establishing the regulations by order in council, however, it is possible for the governor in council to provide for his admission, and that is quite frequently done.
Another example of the kind of thing that is handled in this way would be found in the passage of an order in council to permit the admission to Canada of a Swiss manufacturer who desires to come to this country with certain capital and technical knowledge to establish himself in business here. Under the existing regulations he is inadmissible, but by the passage of an order in council his admission can be authorized.
The whole movement of displaced persons to Canada has been provided for by order in council.
The members of the house will recall that at the beginning of the depression, the government of the day, under the authority of section 38 of the act, passed order in council P.C. 695 of March 21, 1931, which practically prohibited the landing in Canada of immigrants of all classes and occupations except those coming from the British isles and the United States. This order in council was amended from time to time as it became desirable to widen the field of immigration. Therefore, when for the reasons I have mentioned it is desirable to admit persons who are not classed as admissible under this order in council, new orders are passed waiving the prohibition.
As I have said before, there is nothing new about this procedure. It has always been followed.
It might be of interest to hon. members to know-and I am not citing this in any critical

m0od-that during the period from November 1, 1930, to October 23, 1935, two hundred and seventy-five such orders in council were passed in regard to 4,173 persons, waiving the provisions of the restrictive regulations. May I point out that this was during a time when there was great unemployment and there were felt to be very good reasons for restricting immigration. None of these orders was published. But it shows that even in those times there were considered to be that number of cases which were worthy of special treatment.
I should also say a word about the alleged "secrecy" of these orders in council. In fact, of course, there is nothing at all secret about them. When an order in council is of a general character, changing the regulations or affecting categories of persons, that order is published in the Canada Gazette. On the other hand, when the order in council deals with groups of individuals or specific individuals, it is normally considered to be of interest only to the persons immediately concerned and it is not published. Information about it, however, can be obtained by application to the immigration branch.
Perhaps I can summarize what I have said in this way.
There is nothing secret about the immigration orders in council.
There is nothing new about this method of administering the act. It is the procedure that was envisaged when the act was passed and it has been followed by all governments. These orders from 1930 to 1935 were not published or tabled. They were passed in the usual course, as have been those made since.
I think this would be an appropriate time to refer to statements attributed by the press to the hon. member for Lake Centre.
According to the Montreal Gazette of March 9, the hon. member is reported to have taken steps to determine why the federal government has not tabled all special immigration permits, covering cases not covered by the Immigration Act. This statement appears to be confusing two different things. Section 4 of the Immigration Act provides that the minister may issue a written permit authorizing any person to enter Canada, or having entered or landed in Canada, to remain therein without being subject to the provisions of the act. These permits are limited in time; they do not grant and cannot be used to allow permanent entry. The statute requires that they must be reported to the house within thirty days of the opening of the session, and that is always done. The return for the calendar year 1948, as I have already said, was tabled at the beginning of this session, and showed that fifty-six persons, and fifty-six persons
Immigration
only, were granted such permits. Of these twenty were Polish veterans.
With regard to the other category of persons, that is, those who have been admitted by order in council, I have fully explained the situation in the course of the statement I have just made.
But I want to make it absolutely clear that the department has invariably reported all cases of persons admitted by minister's permit as is required by the act, and this year the report, which was required to be made within thirty days, was made within three days, of the opening of the session.
I should like to refer to another statement attributed to the same hon. member. The Ottawa Journal last Tuesday quoted him as saying that by the use of "secret" orders in council, the government may provide an "underground railway by which thousands of aliens are entering the country, completely by-passing the Immigration Act ..." May I say emphatically that it is a complete distortion of the facts to suggest that there are orders in council providing "an underground railway" or "by-passing the Immigration Act". These orders in council have been passed in accordance with the provisions of the act and in accordance with long established practice.
Because of the controversies which have arisen over this, I felt it my duty towards the Canadian people and their representatives in this house to establish the facts in their true light, so that whatever differences there may be as to the wisdom of particular decisions, there may be no further doubt as to the legality of the procedure, and no excuse for allegations that there has been any concealment or secrecy.
I now table the return I have just mentioned.

(a) the resolution for a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war; (b) the resolution for a measure to amend the Agricultural Products Act to extend the operation of the act for a period of one year; (c) the resolution to amend the Canadian Commercial Corporation
Business of the House
Act to provide authority for advances to the corporation by way of loan out of the consolidated revenue fund and to extend the time of operation of the act; (d) the resolution for a measure to provide for the continuance in force of the Foreign Exchange Control Act until sixty days after the commencement of the first session of parliament commencing in the year 1951.
He said: Mr. Speaker, when this notice of motion was drafted I had hoped that by the time it was presented the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne would have been concluded. But the debate has provided opportunity to so many members to bring to the attention of the house matters which they have considered to be of interest that we have not yet concluded the debate, and it may not be concluded today. I shall, therefore, ask one of my colleagues to move, as an amendment to the motion, that if the debate on the address be not concluded at or before the ending of today's sittings, the order of business set out in this motion apply as from Monday until the business referred to thereunder is completed, and that the order of the house of February 21, 1949, continue to apply after it is thus completed.
The reason for making this motion is as follows: As hon. members will have noted, the motion makes reference to four measures. Three of these are referred to in paragraphs (a), (c), and (d), having reference (a) to a continuation for a limited time of certain orders and regulations; (c) a resolution to amend the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act, and
(d)	a measure to provide for the continuation in force of the Foreign Exchange Control Act. These measures are due to expire sixty days after the opening of parliament, or on March 31, 1949, whichever is the earlier. The sixty days expire on March 27. In order to give the house an opportunity to express itself as to whether or not these measures should continue in force after March 27, it is necessary that they be dealt with before that date. Then, by the terms of the statute, the one dealing with agricultural products will expire on March 31, 1949, unless it is extended. There will be only eight or ten sitting days after Monday in which to deal with these matters, and even during those days hon. members may wish to take some little time to express their views about the text of the north Atlantic security pact, which I hope will be tabled early next week, possibly on Tuesday. We have to deal with these matters, and unfortunately it is necessary that we ask that the debate on the address be interrupted again if it is not completed today.
I think the Canadian public are entitled to expect that parliament will deal with these measures and in express terms say whether

Business of the House
or not they are to be continued beyond March 27 and March 31 respectively. I think it is in the public interest that there be an opportunity for parliament to make its views in that regard expressly known, and that matters of this kind should not be allowed to be disposed of by the lapse of time It is for that reason that I put this motion before the house and ask my colleague to add to it an amendment which will make it applicable if the debate on the address is not completed today.

speechtext:
After years of careful study, Mr. Speaker, of certain individuals among the veterans, I have come to be filled with a deep anxiety concerning Canada's treatment of her veterans. I refer to the case of veteran Thomas Harvey of world war II. According to evidence I placed before this house in June, 1948- evidence that, so far as I know, has never been denied or questioned-the following are facts concerning that unfortunate soldier.
Veteran Thomas Harvey, regimental No. D76502 and pension No. 550593, I find was punished without trial by his equals. He was railroaded forcibly into an insane asylum. He was held in that asylum under duress. He was foi; years cheated out of his well-earned pension. He was denied medical treatment to which he was fairly entitled, thereby risking and seriously impairing his health. He was given no chance to contest his case in the courts of the land. He was provided no recourse for redress to any impartial agency. He was intimidated against having recourse to his member of parliament or to parliament.
This is not the only case of that kind which has come to my attention, Mr. Speaker. Careful consideration of this case of veteran Thomas Harvey forces upon one the conclusion that the time has come for the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) to discover for himself, the government and the Canadian people-by a royal commission if need be- the grim, unsightly fact that, in accordance with actual present-day practice in Canada, any Canadian who signs into any of the services of Canada thereby signs a document by which in effect he surrenders, forgoes and forfeits for all the remaining days of his life every one of his fundamental rights and freedoms. In other words, a free Canadian man or woman enlisting in the Canadian forces to defend freedom virtually forgoes for life all possible effective legal claim to those precious inherent freedoms won for him by his fathers through Magna Carta, the petition of right, the bill of rights and every other guarantee reclaimed for Anglo-Saxons through their strenuous thousand years of struggle for liberty.
To anyone who has not studied these cases with some care I know those words sound extreme. But I am afraid that when the facts are all known concerning the way in which scores and scores of veterans of world war I and world war II in Canada have been and are being treated those words will be found to be moderate, and to be a bare, simple expression of the facts as they now exist in Canada.

May I read from Magna Carta:
No freeman shall be seized or imprisoned or dispossessed. or outlawed, or in any way brought to ruin: we will not go against any man nor send against him, save by legal judgment of his peers or by the law of the land.
Again:
To no man will we sell, or deny, or delay right or justice.
A careful consideration of the facts pertaining to Thomas Harvey will, I think, make it abundantly clear to every hon. member that we have fallen far short of Magna Carta, even, in respect of our treatment of certain classes of veterans. I am not saying that a great many of our veterans do not obtain treatment which is quite satisfactory but there is a "no man's land" of veterans. The luckless individuals who happen to find themselves in "no man's land" are in a bad way.	,
We have permitted to grow up in peacetime in Canada a military dictatorship over our veterans, under the name of the Department of Veterans Affairs, including the Canadian pension commission, and the war veterans allowance board. This dictatorship is absolute as far as many people are concerned. In fact, I have evidence to show that employees working under the war veterans allowance board and the Canadian pension commission have rather arrogantly told people that they would not modify their way of treating any given case no matter who asked them to do so, whether it was a member of parliament or anyone else. In due time I will bring evidence to show that that has actually happened in Canada, and within the last year; and I think the evidence I have is dependable.
Let us take a glance at the present-day organizations to which I have referred, namely the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Canadian pension commission and the war veterans allowance board. I asked a question which was answered recently in this house. The question was:
1.	How many former commissioned officers are now employed by D.V.A.?
2.	Of these, how many were (a) brigadiers; (b) colonels or lieutenant-colonels; (c) majors, or officers of equivalent rank in other services?
In a return dated March 7, 1949, for the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Canadian pension commission and the war veterans allowance board, the answer given was as follows:
1.	1,386 former commissioned officers.
2.	(a) 8 brigadiers; (b) 122 colonels, lieutenant-colonels, officers of equivalent rank; (c) 269 majors, officers of equivalent rank.
We might as well face the facts. The Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) both know,-as do a majority of the
The Address-Mr. Blackmore members of this house, I believe-through having been in the army, that during military activities, training and fighting, great bitterness often develops between the men and their officers. Sometimes it is the fault of the officers; sometimes it is the fault of the men; and sometimes it is merely the fault of the situation in which they find themselves. Nevertheless, the bitterness is there.

speechtext: Will the hon. member allow me to make a comment at this particular time?' In the first place, I deny that statement regarding great bitterness. In the second place, as the house knows, all the medical officers, all the nursing sisters, and all the pension doctors in my department are as far as possible men and women who had service. All such medical personnel-both men and women-when serving in the forces were automatically of commissioned rank.

The men who occupy key positions in the Department of Veterans Affairs are men who could have had grudges against certain men in the services or who could be influenced by men who have had grudges against those men, and who could be influenced in their judgment on a given case by such considerations as that. I am not saying they are.

speechtext:
The hon. member would be surprised at how much I know, and we shall just leave it at that. When the time comes that we can get at each other across

The Address-Mr. Blackmore the floor I shall give the hon. member all the evidence that he wants, and perhaps a little more.
The difficulty lies in the fact that there is too much of a stacking of the cards against certain veterans, and I believe that the case of Thomas Harvey well illustrates that point. I wish to make this comment. There must be provided in Canada a set of nonmilitary, nonbiased tribunals, before whom the humblest and weakest veteran can present his case and call in every bit of pertinent evidence, with implicit assurance that every particle of applicable evidence shall be sympathetically weighed on his behalf. That certainly does not exist today. These tribunals must have power to compel the making of appropriate adjustments in favour of the veteran where these are justified.
On June 30, 1948, I put on record a statement prepared by veteran Thomas Harvey. I refer hon. members to Hansard of 1948 at pages 6228 and 6229. The salient facts concerning veteran Harvey's case, as outlined in his statement, will be elicited by answering the twenty-five questions which I asked on June 30, as recorded on pages 6227 and 6228 of Hansard. These questions have never yet been answered. It may be the intention of the department to answer them in this house, but thus far they have not been answered. If the evidence at hand concerning veteran Harvey's experiences is reliable, and it would appear to be so, then it is important that this house and the country should know who are the persons responsible for the wrongs committed against veteran Harvey in the name of Canada.
In order to help the minister to discover these persons, and the nature of their responsibility to the Minister of Veterans Affairs,
I propose to put the following series of questions. These questions are slightly different from the ones which I asked on June 30, but I believe that they go after information which is vital to all Canadians at the present time. Let us bear this in mind. Probably half the members of this house are going to have sons enrolled within the armed forces of Canada within the next two or three years, and there will be tens of thousands of people across Canada who will have sons enrolled in these forces. In the past we have had to worry about having our boys injured in service, or taken sick in service, or killed in service or lost. Now we have the haunting fear that something will happen to them and that they will fall into the clutches of some inner circle in the war veterans allowances department or Canadian pensions commission, and suffer as horrible outrages as those which were endured by Thomas Harvey. I say that it is absolutely unjust, inequitable and injurious 
that Canadian people should have to worry, as men would worry, after hearing about Thomas Harvey.
The following are the questions:
1.	Where is the Captain Haljerston, president of the mess, whom veteran Thomas Harvey had paraded before Major General Price and charged with refusing to obtain medical aid for veteran Harvey sometime between September 8, 1939 and June 10, 1940?
2.	Upon whose recommendation was veteran Harvey sent back to Canada In May or June, 1940?
3.	Upon what grounds was the recommendation made?
4.	Who asked veteran Harvey to sign his discharge?
5.	Who told veteran Harvey that the veteran would receive no treatment for his pains?
6.	Who threatened to keep veteran Harvey in detention until veteran Harvey did sign his discharge without guarantee of suitable treatment for his illness?
7.	To what extent was Captain Haljerston at the bottom of the two outrages against Harvey referred to in questions 5 and 6?
8.	Was veteran Harvey classified as A-l upon enlistment?
He says he was.
9.	Was veteran Harvey classified as category E upon discharge?
He says he was.
10.	Was veteran Harvey X-rayed upon discharge?
He says he was not.
11.	Was veteran Harvey, notwithstanding the facts indicated in questions 8, 9 and 10, told that he did not need treatment?
12.	Who was responsible for this miscarriage of justice?
13.	To what extent was Captain Haljerston at the bottom of this piece of skulduggery?
14.	Who in the D.V.A. refused veteran Harvey treatment for his pains on the grounds that there was nothing wrong with him? Why?
15.	After veteran Harvey had gone to a civilian
hospital and been diagnosed as afflicted with T.B., who refused to grant him treatment in D.V.A. on the grounds that he had been out of the service for more than a year?	.
16.	What facilities are provided by D.V.A. for rectifying for a veteran such crass injustices as are indicated in questions 14 and 15?
17.	Why did not these facilities intervene on behalf of veteran Harvey?
13. By what course of procedure can a veteran now suffering from such a grievance gain redress?
19.	Why was pension granted veteran Harvey in May, 1946?
20.	Why had he not received pension in May, 1944, in May, 1942, in May, 1941?
He had already been discharged as category E after enlisting as category A.
20.	(a) Who refused veteran Harvey pension?
21.	To what extent was Captain Haljerston responsible for this wrong against veteran Harvey and Canada?
22.	Why was veteran Harvey taken under escort from the veterans pavilion to Ste. Anne's when it was known that he was afflicted with T.B.?
22.	(a) Upon whose orders was this done?
23.	Did veteran Harvey get out of Ste. Anne's on condition that he would not fight for his pension or write to parliament about his treatment?
He says he did.

24.	Does this signify that the D.V.A. systematically intimidates veterans of certain classes to discourage them from writing to members of parliament, to discourage them from fighting for their pension rights?
25.	After veteran Harvey left Ste. Anne's was he still denied treatment by D.V.A., although he was haemorrhaging and growing worse?
He says he was.
26.	Was veteran Harvey on May 7, 1948, forcibly taken from St. Hyacinthe, where he was recovering steadily, to Ste. Anne's?
He says he was.
27.	What was the reason?
28.	Who gave the orders?
29 At Ste. Anne's was veteran Harvey locked up for six weeks and held incommunicado?
He says he was.
30.	Upon whose orders?
31.	For what reason?
I do not know how anything more important to the fathers and mothers can possibly be found than these questions and the answers to these questions. The country will expect the minister to answer the twenty-five questions on pages 6227 and 6228 of Hansard of 1948, and the thirty-one questions I have asked today. I suggest that the minister answer these questions early.
I have several other flagrant cases-Stuart Brown is among them. Stuart Brown has written an extended article, very carefully prepared, very thoroughly documented, given in great detail under the title, "They put me in Essondale". This article appeared in the Vancouver Sunday Sun on January 8, January 15, and January 22, 1949. Before this session is over I am going to call for an accounting for the treatment of veteran Brown. Why are there these outrages against veterans? What is the fundamental cause? Is it a fact the government fears Canada is unable to produce enough food for those boys to eat, enough clothes for them to wear, enough shelter to protect them? Is that what is the matter? Or is it a fact they are afraid they cannot raise the money to provide the needs of these veterans?
That is a vital question. That is the point at which that which I am discussing enters into this debate, on the amendment of the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low). That is why I say a change in the method of financing should be found.
May I stop here to assure the minister who sits in the house that I do not wish to complain against him at all. In my judgment he is the victim of circumstances, and he faces a task of such colossal magnitude, in endeavouring to clean up the situation over which he is now called upon to preside, that I doubt if any man alive could do it. It will
The Address-Mr. Blackmore require a great deal more assistance than the efforts of one man. The object of my efforts today is partially that of giving the minister some assistance.
The solution to the problem facing us in connection with veterans is the solution to the problem in connection with old age pensions and a hundred and one other things troubling us in Canada. It is a money question. The whole trouble is one of money.
I am going to suggest the solution lies in social credit, and it is implied in the amendment offered by the hon. member for Peace River.
Before I commence to discuss social credit I should like to pay some attention to certain remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). With this in mind I shall read some of his words as they were reported at page 1341 of Hansard. The hon. member rose and, in a rather assured way-perhaps that word is sufficient-proceeded to tell the house or to imply to the house that he knew all about social credit, that probably he knew quite a lot more about it than hon. members who are fighting for social credit, and that long ago he had discovered that it was fallacious. I hope I am fair to him in this remark, and I shall proceed to read what he said:
The more I read the more I came to the conclusion that while financial reform was necessary, he was going about it at the wrong end-
Referring to Major Douglas-
-that it is not money that counts, but physical assets and goods. The physical assets and goods must precede the distribution of money; otherwise you have merely an inflationary process.
With the second part of his remarks of course we all agree; and the hon. member for Peace River said we believe that. The surprising thing is that the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar would take the trouble to make a remark which, in the light of the knowledge he must have, if he knows anything about social credit, must be considered to be completely inane.
What manner of man is this member for Rosetown-Biggar? He poses as a rather intelligent fellow, rather an able chap. He would like to have people consider him something of a student, and he would hate to be called dishonest.
Having said that, let me point out some of the things the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar has done or has neglected to do since he came to this house in 1935, the same year in which I came.
He has been in the house long enough to know better than to make a remark like the one he made yesterday. The first speech I made in March of 1936 made clear that social

The Address-Mr. Blackmore credit proposes to create money to represent surplus goods and services already on the market. That fact completely stultifies the remark of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. It indicates that either he is not intelligent, or he is not diligent, or he is not honest-one of the three. He may choose whichever of the three undesirable alternatives he wishes. In the first speech I delivered in 1936 I cited the fact that in 1918 the United States produced $60 billion worth of goods-and I wish the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar's friends would call him in.
I wish he were here-I was hoping he would be. I want to talk with him face to face. I said that in 1918 the United States produced $60 billion worth of goods, but distributed among the people only $45 billion worth of purchasing power.
How in the world could a bit of evidence be found which would more clearly illustrate the fact that social credit stands for the monetization of surplus goods? And the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar must have sat right here in the house and heard my speech -although he probably utterly disregarded it, as coming from one of those poor Social Crediters who did not know anything. I believe that probably this year we shall have to have a real collision with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, to find out who does know more-he, or the Social Crediters. I must say he has not shown up very promisingly thus far. He does not show in a very favourable light, considering what he said yesterday.
The figures I have given will be found in the report of the bureau of economic research, No. 2, for 1922. This is a United States document, and is obtainable in the House of Commons library. I wonder if, when the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar was studying social credit, he read the Douglas books. I wonder if he read Maurice Colboume's two remarkable books, the first of which is "Unemployment or war" and the second "Economic Nationalism"? I wonder if he ever read Charles Marshall Hattersley's "This Age of Plenty"? If he had read any of these he would have had it impressed upon him, and it would have been made painfully clear to him so clear that even he could have seen, or could not have failed to see-that what was in mind was the creation of money to enable people to buy surplus goods; he would have seen that the difficulty arises out of the shortage of purchasing power which develops naturally in our modern economy, in which we have an abundance.
Time and again since 1936 I have repeated the truth which I have indicated, and I have 

done so in the presence of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. He has had Hansard; he could have read it. If he did not have the time, probably he could have had his secretary read it.
Now let me illustrate further. I have pointed out, too, that the reason the depression hurt the United States so painfully was that between 1929 and 1934 eight billions of dollars in purchasing power, of a total of $23 billion, had been withdrawn in the United States. Naturally it was the shortage of purchasing power which caused the falling of prices and which caused the depression in the United States, so far as its technical and physical aspects were concerned. In the Dominion of Canada in that same period over $930 million was withdrawn. This indicated quite clearly that while we were in the depths of the depression, one for which my Liberal friends love to blame the Conservative party, we were suffering from a shortage of purchasing power, and surplus of goods. Will some of the intimate friends of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar take that copy of Hansard, read it to him, and point out the words I have just mentioned?
As I have declared three or four times in the house, the fundamental cause of the depression in the United States was the fact that within her own economy the United States had a shortage of purchasing power, as was indicated by the figures of production and purchasing power in 1918.
Between the years 1920 and 1929 the United States lent abroad vast quantities of money to enable people abroad to buy her goods. Thus she maintained a level of prosperity, or apparent prosperity, in her own economy. The trouble was she had a shortage of purchasing power and too many goods. Let the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar take note of that-too many goods. Once more I do hope he is able to read what I say this time. The United States lent money abroad so that people could buy her goods which her own people could not buy, goods for which they did not have the money to pay.
In 1928 it began to dawn on United States authorities that perhaps it was not safe to lend money abroad to enable people to buy their goods. So they discontinued lending abroad; and that fact caused the depression.
I am sure the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and his colleagues need to read deeply of these matters before they can attempt to be the wise men they claim to be. I am sure the Liberals have not read deeply enough of these matters because they do not know anything about what it is all about. I am sure the Conservatives do not know. They

do not know as much as the Liberals, judging from the way they have been talking in the house.
The simple matter is that if we are going to begin to deal with the causes of our trouble instead of just the symptoms, if we are going to begin to discuss a policy that will solve our problems instead of just throwing smoke screens around and scattering red herrings on the trail, we have to get down to the fundamental causes of the phenomena which afflict our generation.
The fundamental cause of the phenomena which afficted us in 1929 was the shortage of purchasing power in the United States economy which the United States endeavoured to rectify by lending abroad, just as she is doing today through the Marshall plan. When she ceased to lend abroad she was in for the depression into which she descended with such fearful rapidity. She will do the same thing again unless a remedy is applied to the fundamental cause of all these troubles.
If the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar or any one else desires to read up on this matter rather than just take what the Social Crediters say, I would suggest to him that he read "The United States in the World Economy", to be found in the parliamentary library. If the hon. member cannot find a copy down there I will lend him mine if he comes to me. I can show him where he will find the facts. He will discover that what I have said about the causes of the depression in the United States is true. "The United States in the World Economy" is a United States public document which was prepared by a committee which was especially appointed to examine into the causes of the trouble which came on to the United States in the depression.
The United States and Canada are now approaching a surplus position. That is the reason why I asked the questions I did the other day of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). If we are approaching a surplus position in Canada in connection with a considerable number of commodities, then we are on the verge of a depression. We shall have to make fundamental adjustments in our national economy in order to enable us to distribute the purchasing power necessary to absorb those surpluses or they will become vexatious in several different ways. We must have a distribution of purchasing power if a depression is to be avoided.
I am going to refer once more to "The United States in the World Economy" a carefully prepared document. Is the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar prepared to face the facts, now that I have brought them out? Are the members of the C.C.F. prepared to face the facts? Does the hon. member for Rose-
The Address-Mr. Blackmore town-Biggar dare to face the facts? I suggest that several of his most trusted members take him aside and suggest to him that he read what I have said in this speech this afternoon and then explain himself to them. Let me tell him that if he does face the facts he and his party will have to stop talking their nonsense about private enterprise failing, because it is the success of private enterprise in producing goods that brings about surpluses.
Let me point out another fundamental principle which I am afraid has eluded the intelligence of a number of them. No industry is designed to distribute purchasing power, be that industry a coal mine or a farm or any other kind of industry. Industry is designed to produce goods. When an industry produces ample goods, it succeeds rather than fails. The fact that we have produced surpluses so many times is the best evidence that private enterprise has succeeded superbly in producing goods. But private enterprise cannot distribute purchasing power enough to enable people to buy the goods it produces. Private enterprise, and even a government-owned industry, could not afford to spend as much money in producing its goods as it receives for the goods.

possibly find for the problems which confront us today, for the ills from which we are suffering in Canada today and throughout the world, is to be found in the social credit proposals, and the only accurate analysis of the situation is the social credit analysis."
Just before I close I want to read into the record, as evidence of the truth of what I have been saying with regard to the need for adjustment in the United States, a passage from "The United States in the World Economy." This is to be found on page vi, and it reads:
A world economic structure organized on the basis of equal treatment and with large scope for free enterprise cannot be maintained in the face of such reductions in the supply of dollars as have occurred in our international transactions in the past. Unless the supply of dollars is more adequate-
I direct the attention of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar to these words:
-to meet foreign requirements, other countries will assuredly insist on their rights to exercise a close selective control over the use of the amounts available and to promote more intensive relations with third countries under preferential trading arrange-

ments. Unless dollars are made available with greater regularity than in the past, it would be both unjust and unwise to demand the removal of restraints and controls largely designed to protect the internal economies of other countries against external shock and pressure.
That is dealing with the international situation, but here is what is said about the internal situation, the problem of distributing purchasing power:
On the solution of these problems, through maintenance of a high and reasonably stable level of economic activity in the United States, the interests of this country, and of other countries, are most clearly and indisputably united.
There is only one way in the world in which the United States or Canada can keep her economy stable, and that is by continually introducing into the hands of consumers sufficient purchasing power to enable them to buy the goods they can produce. The only possible solution to the world's difficulties is to be able to put into the hands of the have-not people the money which is necessary to enable them to buy those goods which the more happy countries can produce.
Because of the evidence and of the facts which I have brought forward, I intend to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low).

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I propose to say a few words about the question of freight rates, and I do so for two reasons. First of all I believe that there is great urgency about the matter. It is now admitted in most parts of Canada that there are great inequalities in our Canadian freight rate structure. Unfortunately each delay in dealing with these inequalities makes the position just that much worse. Therefore the time element is of great importance. My second reason for dealing with the subject today is that I fear there will be no other opportunity before the Easter adjournment, and possibly for the remainder of the session. I say that for this reason. Not only is there nothing coming up on the order paper which would open up a debate on the subject, but a royal commission on transportation has been set up, and I expect that once that commission commences its hearings anyone who rises in the house and tries to debate the question of freight rates will be met with the objection that the matter is under the consideration of the courts. In effect, an iron curtain will then be drawn over the question, and it will be impossible to have effective debate.
In approaching the subject at this time I believe it is necessary to bring up to date the record of what has been happening, and to see that the record is kept straight. It is also necessary to make clear to the house,

and to the country, that the removal of the inequities, of the discrimination, is still a long way off; also that it is necessary to ask that the functions of the two bodies which are supposed to be dealing with the question of freight rates, the royal commission on transportation and the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, be much more clearly defined; at the present time there is great uncertainty across the country as to the respective functions of the two bodies. I think it is also necessary to demand that the government face its responsibilities on the freight rate question.
There is a reference to the matter in the speech from the throne, reading as follows:
A royal commission has been appointed to inquire into and report upon all questions of economic policy within the jurisdiction of parliament arising out of the operation and maintenance of national transportation.
That, of course, refers to the royal commission. Then the paragraph goes on:
Together with the findings of the investigation by the board of transport commissioners, the report of the royal commission should furnish parliament and the government with the basis for a sound transportation policy.
Here we have the government handing on the obligation to determine policy on railroad transportation not to one commission or board, which is the usual practice, but actually to two boards. We have two bodies being asked to do the job which the government should do for itself.
What is the record on the. question? On October 11, 1946, the railways applied for a flat increase in freight rates of thirty per cent. I suppose there were very few people in the country who did not believe that the railways were entitled to a reasonable increase because of the rising costs in all the activities of the country. The application for an increase was opposed by seven of the provinces, the three maritime provinces on the east coast, Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, and the four western provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. Those seven provinces were the ones primarily concerned with any increase in freight rates.
The other two provinces, Quebec and Ontario, are not so much concerned about fail charges. The distances that freight has to be hauled in those two provinces are much shorter. Then, too, there is very efficient road and water transportation which is in direct competition with the railroads, and which has served throughout the years to keep rail rates down; and has resulted in fact in the full rates permitted in Ontario and Quebec not being charged in many cases. As I have said,
. The Address-Mr. Green these two provinces were not directly concerned with the increase in the freight rates.
British Columbia was in the unfortunate position of being more concerned than any other province because the people of that province pay the highest rate of all by reason of what is known as the mountain differential, which takes the prairie rate and adds to that another quarter. It costs as much to haul freight a mile in British Columbia as it does to haul it a mile and a quarter in the prairie provinces, and the prairie rates are higher, of course, than the rates in Ontario and Quebec, or in the maritime provinces.
The board of transport commissioners held many sittings across Canada, and finally on March 30, 1948, handed down a judgment which allowed a flat increase of twenty-one per cent as against the increase of thirty per cent which had been requested by the railways. In their judgment they held that the freight rates must pay not only for the costs of operating the railways but also such charges as income taxes, dividends, fixed charges, depreciation and surplus, although a portion of those charges came from other earnings such as hotel earnings, shipping earnings, and various other services supplied by the railways. The Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company is another example, it being a subsidiary of the Canadian Pacific Railway. The judgment could be put into effect upon three days' notice, which meant that the increase of twenty-one per cent could be made by the railways after that time had passed.
Great dissatisfaction was expressed immediately by the seven provinces which had been involved in the hearings. I have here the different wires that were sent to the cabinet requesting mainly that the increase of twenty-one per cent be suspended for a period of thirty days in order that the different premiers might get together and decide what they would do about appealing the judgment. For example, I shall read from the, wire sent by the premier of Manitoba, who is now the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) in the government. In his wire we find these words:
The provinces which oppose the application desire the opportunity to meet and consider the judgment and to formulate their grounds of appeal, and it would be manifestly unjust to allow the higher rates to go into effect before they have had this opportunity.
Those seven provinces were in this position, that the only appeal they had from the judgment of the board of transport commissioners was to the cabinet. There is no other appeal from a decision of the transport board. On April 7 the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), speaking in this house, announced

The Address-Mr. Green that the government refused to suspend the operation of the judgment, and went on to say that the government had decided to order the board of transport commissioners to conduct a general rate inquiry. That was the answer given by the government to the seven provinces. I have here the order in council passed on that date, P.C. 1487, which contains the instructions to the board of transport commissioners concerning this general rate inquiry, and I read the material part of it, as follows:
... it is therefore advisable that the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada be directed to make a thorough investigation of the rates structure of railways and railway companies which are under the jurisdiction of parliament, with a view to the establishment of a fair and reasonable rates structure which will, under substantially similar circumstances and conditions, be equal in its application to all persons and localities so as to permit the freest possible interchange of commodities between the various provinces and territories of Canada and the extension of Canadian trade both foreign and domestic, having due regard to the needs of agriculture nd the other basic industries.
It goes on to exempt from that inquiry the statutory provisions, which I believe are the maritime freight rates and the Crowsnest rates, both of which are in existence by reason of statute. In effect the government on April 7 last admitted that there were inequalities in the freight rate structure. Hon. members were very much concerned. The minister was asked how long it would take to complete this general inquiry and this was his answer, to be found at page 2718 of Hansard for April 7:
It may take a year, or it may take two years. That will depend upon the dispatch with which the board can get across the country.
Because the minister's statement was not considered satisfactory, that same day an amendment was moved to a motion to go into supply, by means of which the whole freight rate question was brought before the house. It was also a matter of the greatest interest across the country. For example, I have the 'leading editorial from the Vancouver Sun of April 9, 1948; and as the minister knows that newspaper is a consistent supporter of this government. In the editorial I find this paragraph:
This government has given the victims of regional rate discrimination not the slightest grounds to believe that it is interested in inequalities as such. It is interested, however, in shutting up the roars of protest evoked by a twenty-one per cent magnification of the injustices.
That was a very good word, I think, to apply to these increases, considering the discrimination which existed before. The debate was adjourned on April 7 and resumed on April 13, when the minister took part. At page 2904 of Hansard for that date he dealt 
with the question of the length of time it would take the board of transport commissioners to complete this general inquiry. He said:
In order that there will be no further misunderstanding on this question may I say that I conferred with the chief commissioner of the board and asked him how long in his opinion it would take to complete this investigation. He said that because of the circumstances which had changed in the economy of this country from the time that the judgment was handed down in 1927-
There the chairman was referring to a previous general inquiry.
-it would require an absolute minimum of six months in which to complete the investigation, and that it would probably be completed within a year.
Then on April 15 the board of transport commissioners issued a directive, which stressed the need for speedy action. For example, it says:
The Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada, in order to carry out as expeditiously as possible the direction of the above recited order in council-
That is the one from which I read a few moments ago.
-hereby invites provincial governments and other authorities, boards of trade, chambers of commerce and other interested parties to submit to the board any statement of facts under which it is claimed that unjust discrimination, or undue or unreasonable preference or advantage, or prejudice or disadvantage, or unfair treatment exists against or in favour of any locality, province or region by reason of the present rate structure.
The directive goes on to say that submissions should be filed not later than May 25, 1948, and that the railways would be given until June 30, 1948, to file answers. Then it goes on further:
The purpose of this notice is to put the board, as early as possible-
I point out that throughout this directive the board is stressing speed.
-in possession of any and all complaints against the existing rate structure, and to specifically direct attention to the subject matter of such complaints, with a view of considering what changes, adjustments and redistribution in rate incidence may be necessary to correct the defects complained of.
The board desires to proceed with the investigation and to hold such public hearings as may be deemed necessary with the least possible delay, and to conduct the same in a manner most calculated to secure a complete and systematic development of all material facts.
That directive was issued just about eleven months ago. Eleven months have gone by, and I believe as yet not one brief has been filed by a provincial government. There have been no hearings. It looks as though this general rate inquiry has just been pigeonholed in the meantime.

May I interrupt the hon. gentleman? The application for the removal

of the mountain differential, which came from British Columbia, has been heard since that time, following that directive.
I am going to deal with that in a moment.

Is that not so? The hon. gentleman has made the statement that nothing has been done under that directive, and I am saying now that the application of British Columbia has been heard. Is that not right?

The minister is not right, because the directive to which I referred has to do with the general rate inquiry. It quotes the order in council issued on April 7, and deals only with the general rate inquiry. The application of British Columbia for the removal of the mountain differential was an entirely separate application.

No, it was not. I do not want to be interjecting, as my hon. friend interjected during my speech, and if he thinks I should not I will sit down. But I believe he should be fair. The mountain differential is a part of the whole rate-base structure.
The minister will understand as I go along. I will deal with that point.
I did not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman unduly.

This general rate inquiry has not been held, and unfortunately the discrimination continues. Of course that discrimination was accentuated by the 21 per cent increase, because it meant that where an unfair rate was being charged that rate went up 21 per cent, which was more than the 21 per cent on a lower rate.
Then in spite of the formula therein to which I referred a few moments ago, which said that the freight rates had to bear all these various charges, the minister in his speech in this house also vigorously defended the judgment of the board of transport commissioners. I would refer you, Mr. Speaker, to page 2900 of last year's Hansard; it was on April 13. As reported at page 2900 of Hansard of 1948 the minister said:
The board gave careful consideration to all the arguments that were put before it. They sat for almost fourteen months.
He went on to say how careful they had been in holding hearings in all parts of Canada. Then he said:
There are six commissioners on the board at the present time.
The Address-Mr. Green Then he uses these words, which are the key words supporting the point I am now making:
The board through the chief commissioner has delivered a clear and outstanding judgment in this case.
He went on to refer to the various commissioners, and to point out how much each of these commissioners knew about the railway question, arguing that, because they knew so much about it, therefore their judgment was right. But he was not content with that.
The words speak for themselves.

Yes, they certainly do. The words shout for themselves. The minister went on to explain about the board's experts. He said they were fine experts and therefore the judgment must be right. The tragedy of the minister's action was this. In this country we have, or are supposed to have, cabinet solidarity. The minister spoke for the cabinet, and the cabinet was the only body to which persons could appeal against this judgment of the board of transport commissioners. In effect the Minister of Transport (Mr. Chevrier), for the cabinet, prejudged any appeal that the seven provinces might take.
He went further. The other day he was praising this royal commission. I would refer hon. members to page 2906 of Hansard of 1948, the same day, where we find what he thought about a royal commission then. He said:
X say to the house that if we were to appoint a royal commission or other body to investigate the inequalities of the freight rates structure in Canada this is what would happen. The royal commission or other body would come to the government and say, "We are ready to proceed with the case. Give us the technical assistance: give us the experts." We would have to reply, "We know of only two groups of people in this country who are able to give you the technical evidence and assistance you require, and those two groups are to be found in the board of transport commissioners." Those groups are, first, the bureau of economics of the board of transport commissioners, and second, the traffic experts of that board, the one composed of a personnel of forty and the other of a personnel of twenty. That being the case what would be the use of asking four, five or six men, not nearly as conversant with this question as are the members of the board of transport commissioners, and who to my mind would not have the same knowledge of the circumstances as the board, to carry out such an investigation? I say to the house therefore that the members of the board, four of whom are from provinces other than Ontario and Quebec, are better qualified and equipped to deal with this question than would be the members of a specialized board or commission of some land or other.
That is the minister less than a year ago. On the same day, by the way, the leader of the opposition moved an amendment-which will be found at page 2915, and which

The Address-Mr. Green expressed the position of the Progressive Conservative party-in these words:
. . . regrets the government's failure to secure the removal of inequalities and discriminations in the Canadian railway freight rates structure before the imposition of a horizontal increase of twenty-one per cent-an increase which is bound to intensify the aforesaid inequalities and discriminations . . .
Then it went on to regret the refusal of the government to give the provinces thirty days in which to consider an appeal.
That carries the picture up to April 13, 1948. An interesting series of events followed in that year. On April 26 the seven provincial premiers again protested to the cabinet. They were in the position of having had their appeal prejudged by the Minister of Transport on the floor of this house. Obviously, in the nature of things, they would not expect much help from the cabinet. They asked then that a royal commission be set up; and they did not ask for a royal commission just to investigate the transportation question. They actually asked to have set up a royal commission which would act as an appeal body from the judgment of the board of transport commissioners. They also asked for the suspension of the twenty-one per cent increase in the meantime, and went so far as to say that, if the railways were hard-pressed financially during the time that this matter was being considered, the government should subsidize the railways. On April 29, British Columbia filed a claim for the removal of the mountain differential. That was a new case which they filed on that date. This claim has been heard, but the decision has not yet been handed down.
Then on July 1, some two months later, the Prime Minister (Mr. King) advised the seven provinces that he was refusing a royal commission and that there could be no suspension of the twenty-one per cent increase. On July 14 there was a wage increase of seventeen cents an hour across the board. On July 20 the provinces again appeared before the cabinet. At this time they filed their appeal from the decision of the board, and again asked for a royal commission. Four days later, on July 24, the royal commission was refused. Four days after that again, on July 28, the railways applied for a further increase-that is, on top of the increase of twenty-one per cent.
I believe their second application was for a fifteen per cent interim increase and a twenty per cent permanent increase. But I am told that now the argument is for a twenty per cent flat increase over and above the twenty-one per cent increase granted previously.
Early in August the government party held a convention here in Ottawa. Among the resolutions passed by that convention-we 
were told it was against the wishes of the cabinet, and it certainly must have been against the wishes of the Minister of Transport-was one advocating the setting up of a royal commission on transportation. On September 17 the announcement was made that there was to be a royal commission. In other words, the Minister of Transport was then overruled for the first time.
On September 27 and 28 the provinces argued before the cabinet their appeal from the decision of the board. The Minister of Transport was not present at that time. He was representing Canada at a conference in Europe. It was a good thing that he was away, in view of the speech he had made on April 13. In any event, eleven other ministers heard the appeal by those seven provinces. On October 14 the eleven members of the cabinet handed down a judgment which will be found in "Canadian Railway and Transport Cases," volume 62, at page 273. That judgment upset the formula which had been laid down by the board. I will quote to the house the material paragraph, which reads as follows:
The committee are favourably impressed with the view-
That is, the cabinet.
-that income derived by the railways from sources other than their railway transportation operations should not be entirely excluded by the board in determining the corporate needs of the railways. The payment of fixed charges and income taxes are corporate obligations of corporations as such, and the incomes of corporations, whatsoever their source, are liable therefor; provisions to be made for dividends and a surplus are likewise corporate needs and should be so considered. For these reasons, the committee are of the opinion that some portion of the corporate needs should be borne by the income derived from nonrailway operations.
The cabinet referred the judgment back to the board of transport commissioners. The headnote reads that it is to be referred back for consideration by the board of the claims set forth in the petition by the provinces, and that consideration "should take place concurrently with and in relation to the pending application by the railways for a further increase in freight rates." Then the following footnote appears:
The result of this order in council is that the increase of 21 per cent in freight rates authorized by the board in the general increase case 1946-48 will remain in effect unless and until altered by the board by means of an adjustment which may be made in the course of its disposition of a pending application for a further increase of 20 per cent in freight rates.
The Minister of Transport was clearly wrong in April, 1948. He was proved wrong by the fact that in October, 1948, his colleagues found the judgment of the board of transport commissioners in error. Since October, 1948, the board has been hearing

these two applications; reconsidering the application for a 21 per cent increase on the basis suggested by the cabinet, and also hearing for the first time the application for an additional 20 per cent increase. All the time, Mr. Speaker, the discrimination continues and it will be made worse, as I pointed out, by any flat increase. There is no sign of a general rates inquiry by the board of transport commissioners.
In the meantime, on December 29, a royal commission on transportation was appointed. Its powers, obviously, conflict with the powers given to the board of transport commissioners to hold a general rates inquiry. In addition to a repetition of the powers given to the board for such inquiry, power is given to this royal commission to review the Railway Act, and to review the capital structure of the Canadian National Railways. Various other powers are given to them, with the one proviso contained in the last paragraph of the order in council setting up the commission, which reads as follows:
That the scope of this commission shall not extend to the performance of functions which, under the Railway Act, are within the exclusive jurisdiction of the board of transport commissioners.
There is no proviso there concerning the statutory freight rates, namely, the maritime freight rates and the Crowsnest rates. They are not excepted from the powers of the royal commission. It may well be that these statutory rates will be lost as a result of the hearings of the royal commission. Furthermore there is no sign of the commencement of the hearings of this royal commission. There has already been a delay of six months. In September of last year it was announced that a commission would be appointed, and when the commission was set up on December 29 press dispatches stated that the job of the commission would take the better part of a year, with public hearings across the country starting perhaps in two months from the announcement of the appointment of the commission. That would mean in March. The press dispatch goes on to say:
It is not expected a report will be received from the commissioners befo^p 1950.
The other day I asked the minister when the hearings were to commence and he said the intention had been that they would commence in May-
No, by the end of April.

Surely the end of April would be the beginning of May, or pretty close to it. He said that it had been thought the commission would be ready to proceed by
The Address-Mr. Green the end of April. He went on to say, as reported at page 1062 of Hansard:
Since then I have been informed that provinces have sought some delay in order to prepare their cases.
I point out that there has already been a delay of six months.
It would appear, Mr. Speaker, that the royal commission must first sit and report, because they are instructed to review the Railway Act. The royal commission having reported, if any changes are to be made in the Railway Act, these will have to be put through parliament. After that has been done the board of transport commissioners will have to decide on rates. They would obviously be foolish to try now to set up a new basis of rates, because that job has been handed on to the royal commission. This double set-up, this business of two boards, means more delay; it means more expense; and of course it means that the discriminations continue, unless the railways themselves get soft-hearted and remove them.

In doing so, I should like to assure my Social Credit friends that my comments will be as bereft of chiding criticism, if one can call it that, as I can possibly make them. I have a certain affinity, if I may use the word, with my Social Credit friends. I shall be careful of my words and say that we are both descended from the same social stratum of society, and that consequently we see the same kind of people and to a large extent meet the same conditions. For that reason, if for no other, I have no wish to be either unfair or acrimonious in any remarks I make.
The subamendment, however, is one which this party, I regret, cannot support. It contains three sections, the first of which is an expression of regret that the government has shown studied indifference to social credit financial proposals. The secorfd is a regret that the government has failed to take up the social credit challenge to debate in the house certain aspects of social credit. Surely no such proposals were ever made a part of a want of confidence resolution. What does it matter if the government has not done those things.
Then, the last section is a regret that the government has not made legislative provision for the maintenance of purchasing power for the distribution of goods and services. All of us would agree with that. But if the assumption is that that could only be done, or must be done, by the application of social credit principles, then we cannot agree with it.
Yesterday my leader said the trouble today was not one of a scarcity of money, but a maldistribution of money. As a matter of fact up to a very few months ago it was not a scarcity of money, but too much money.
We agree with that.

If you agree with it, and if that was the condition two months or six months ago, the question is not that there is less money today than there are goods. As a matter of fact the processes of production distribute always in wages, salaries, rent and profits enough money to consume the goods produced.
Never in your life.

Yes, that is the Social Credit argument. They assert one thing and I assert the opposite. And while I am not a Daniel, or any of the major or even the minor prophets, I am prepared to put my opinion against theirs any time. As I shall develop my argument I shall have something to say along that line.
I maintain, and I think every economist of any note anywhere maintains, that the trouble with the capitalist system, with so-called free enterprise, is that it does not distribute equitably enough the fruits of industry so that the people can be provided with the clothing, food and shelter they need through our productive processes. That is the fact. But the reason it does not do that is because it is not its purpose to do that. The purpose of industry is to produce profits for the owners of industry. The more that is put into wages or into any other costs, the less goes into profits. If we do not understand that, I do not believe we can understand anything about our economic system. And until we understand that we will not understand how to apply remedies.
The hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) complained yesterday, as he has on several other occasions-if "complained" is the right word-about his inability to make the members in the house understand the principles of social credit. I have listened to the hon. member since 1935, and the more I listen to him the more confused I am. I am free to say that perhaps that is not his fault; it may be mine. I find however that I can understand other people when they are talking; I can understand what they mean. But I cannot understand the hon. member for Lethbridge or the others in the Social Credit party who deal with the theory of social credit; they are not understandable to me.
Give us an example.
I shall do that.
Give us your amendment of 1935.

Speaking in the house on March 12, 1947, the hon. member for Lethbridge said, as reported at page 1309 of Hansard:
Up to the present time there has been the danger, when banks have lent money, that they could not get their money back. It is obvious that with debt-free money going into circulation among the people the banks would have a far better chance of having their loans repaid. In many cases the loans would be partly if not wholly repaid with debt-free money. That is one way in which the debt-free money would be cancelled out of circulation. So there would not be the danger of too much of it being in circulation.
If that means anything at all, it means that bank loans-in other words, debt money- are to be paid with debt-free money which, when the bankers receive it, they are going to cancel out so that there will not be too much money in circulation. If that makes sense to anyone I should like him to hold up his hand and then to explain it to the house. It does not make sense to me. Then we have this paragraph:
The banks lend money for production purposes but not to pay interest. But interest is necessary to encourage the banks to lend money.
In other words, debt money is necessary to encourage the banks to lend debt money. Then it continues:
The banks also never lend money to pay a profit. If we are to continue under our system of interest and profits the finest way to enable us to carry it on is to have debt-free money which can supply means for the payment of interest and profits. That is another way to cancel debt-free money out of circulation.
There again, when you pay debt-free money to pay interest and to pay profit, then the person receiving it cancels it. If he cancels it out, what has he got?
Nothing.
Well, that is social credit. I have been trying to understand that sort of thing for the last fourteen years.
Page the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine).

If the hon. member for Cariboo understands it, he was never able to make me understand it.
Then, again, my hon. friends charge the socialists and the C.C.F. with favouring controls and regulations. They are fearful if that sort of thing is allowed to creep in we will not be able to control it. As the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) said last night, bad men will get into almost any organization, and may take over control.

I think I can understand English. I have not time to read much more, but the following is found on page 210:
Wage rates in all organized industries will be reduced by 25 per cent where such reduction does not involve a loss to the wage-earner exceeding 20 per cent of the sums received in the form of national dividend. The wage rates ruling in 1928 to be taken as the basis against which the reduction would be made.
Any trade union violating a wage agreement to render its membership liable to suspension of national dividend, and any employers' organization committing a similar offence, to be liable to suspension of price assistance or wage reductions.
If you put a program like that into effect, and I submit that that is the only extant program of the social credit movement, without an iron-clad dictatorship you will be doing something that has never been done before.
That is just the plan for Scotland.

If it is good enough for Scotland it ought to be good enough for any place else. My hon. friends remind me of the minister who had been brought into a new parish. He had been there for six months or so and had never heard any comment on his sermons. One day he asked one of the elders how he thought he was getting along, whether they were satisfied with his sermons, and the elder replied, "Don't worry, the members of this congregation did not know what sin was until you came here." Let me say again that despite what the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) said this afternoon the industries of Canada do distribute purchasing power.
Incidentally.

As a matter of fact any useful work that they do is incidental. It is not their purpose to do useful work for the community; their purpose is to produce profits for the shareholders. If you are selling shares or stock in a company no one will ask you what useful service the company is doing for the community; but they will want to see the balance sheet for last year. If the balance sheet shows a loss, no matter what useful purpose the company is performing they will not buy. That is proof positive of what I say is the purpose of private industry. I regret that we cannot vote for the subamendment.
I should like to say a few words in regard to the amendment moved by the official opposition. This amendment expresses want of confidence in the government and I think it has been referred to as a straight want of confidence motion. It is customary when a member of the house moves a motion of want of confidence for him to give his reasons for moving the motion. The leader of the opposition did that before moving his amendment. When the leader of the C.C.F. party moved the amendment to the amendment, which has been disposed of, he accused the government of failure to deal effectively with two matters; natural products marketing, and national health insurance. We could have included half a dozen other items of government policy, but we have been in the house long enough to know that, if you put a thing in an amendment once you are not allowed to refer to it in an amendment again. We want to move several votes of want of confidence in the government before this session is over, and we are leaving ourselves as free as we can.
The point is that the official opposition voted against the amendment to the amendment although our amendment left the want of confidence part intact. It did not interfere with it at all. Having voted against it, we can only assume that the official opposition are satisfied with the government's marketing policy, and that they are satisfied with the government's policy on national health insurance.

I have every reason to believe that when the next election is over and we come back here to the house I shall be asked to become Minister of Finance. If I should accept, my first step will be to tell the private banks that we intend to discontinue their charters and to assign all their branches and subsidiaries to the Bank of Canada.
