I shall never forget the statement of our former Prime Minister, now the hon. member for Glengarry (Mr. Mackenzie King), in 1935, that once a nation lost control of its currency and credit all else would be idle and futile. Nor shall I forget the words of one of the old financiers, who said, "Give me control of the currency and credit and I care not who makes the nation's laws." We live in an age in which science and invention have improved the old methods of production, but we are still following the orthodox methods of finance. We have seen Canada's debt built up during wartime to the astronomical figure of sixteen billion dollars, on most of which we are paying interest, and we are told we will continue to pay interest on this money until we go to join our ancestors. So I think it is about time the government really took a hand in seeing what makes the clock go round as far as finance is concerned. We can make all the speeches we like in this house; words will not mean anything. It is action we need, and action now. I remember when I took over a municipality which was being run by some of these bureaucrats, with the money of the people being squandered here and there. Before I go on with what I really want to say tonight, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make brief reference to a number of statements that were made by the hon. member for Vancouver East

(Mr. Maclnnis). I want to congratulate him upon the orderly way in which he made a criticism of certain proposals that we have put forward from time to time. But I was surprised at his attitude to the principles of social credit when he said he could not understand them even after studying them for some fourteen years. He even went so far as to say that the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine) had not been able to convert him. I am satisfied that the hon. member for Vancouver East must be suffering from a serious relapse.
I do not think he is getting old; it certainly cannot be his age; but I cannot understand how he can say that he does not understand these principles when apparently he understood them quite clearly in 1935. I should like to quote, in order to refresh his memory, an amendment that he seconded on March 26, 1935. The motion was moved by Mr. Coote and seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East. Let me read the amendment, as reported at page 2138 of Hansard of 1935:
That the amendment be amended by striking out all the words after the word "Canada'' and adding thereto the following:
"and would appear to be based upon the assumption that poverty and debt are inevitable conditions within the country;
and whereas the real and potential wealth of the nation, based upon our natural resources and our capacity to produce, is such as to make possible an abundant provision for all the requirements of our people;
Therefore, this house is of the opinion that the government should take immediate action to insure the fullest and most equitable distribution possible of our socially-created wealth and that, as a first step in this direction, the measures which may be necessary to meet the pressing needs of the farmers and the unemployed should be financed-
And mark this well.
-by the social credit of Canada, thus avoiding a further increase in the debt burden of the country.
The hon. member for Vancouver East took exception to the statement by the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) advocating that debt-free money could be used to reduce the debt. He thought that was a weird suggestion. Yet in 1935 he advocated that social credit should be used for the purpose of expanding certain services without any expansion of debt.
He has a convenient memory.

As I say, the hon. gentleman seems to be suffering a relapse. The hon. member also implied that we in this group were opposed to all controls. Yet on every occasion when a motion has been made in this house to grant the government continuation of emergency power to exercise certain controls, we have always voted for that motion in order that any absolutely necessary controls could be continued. The stand
The Address-Mr. Quelch that we have always taken is that we are opposed to controls for control's sake. We are opposed to the idea of continually controlling, unnecessarily, the lives of the people.
I will give one or two examples of the type of controls that I dislike. During the war we had the wartime prices and trade board.
I am of the opinion that some frustrated fashion expert got into that board. All his life, apparently he had wanted to have the power to make men change their methods of dress. The fashion experts have always been able to get the women to change their methods of dress, to make them pull up their skirts one day and let them down the next. But they have never been able to get men to change their method of wearing pants. So a measure was put into force which said that men would have to take the cuffs off the bottom of their pants. It might be argued that by so doing there would be a saving of a little bit of cloth. One day I went into a store on Sparks street in order to get a pair of semi-finished flannels. They were not hemmed on the bottom. There was enough material on the bottom with which to make cuffs. So I asked the manager, or the man who was serving in the store, to finish them with cuffs. Oh no, he said, that is against the regulations of the wartime prices and trade board. I said, what are you going to do with the cloth? He said, cut it off. I said, what for? He said, to throw it away. I said, surely that would be a waste of cloth; surely they could turn it up into cuffs. He said, no, we will have to cut it off and turn it up underneath. But, he said, if you like, you can take the pants away as they are and turn them up yourself. What kind of silly control was that?
Then again control was exercised over the kind of lapels you wore, and the kind of pockets you wanted. For years I had been in the habit of getting inside pockets in my vest. No, I could not have them; it took extra work. I said, all right, put only two pockets on the outside and put one on the inside. No, they could not do that. It was against the controls. It is that kind of silly control that makes people angry. If any decided benefit accrues from the controls, or if the controls are necessary to the welfare of the country, the people will not object. But just the minute a bunch of bureaucrats start interfering unnecessarily with the peoples' way of life, the people will object.
For some strange reason the hon. member for Vancouver East objected to Major Douglas' plan of assessing the value of human beings. Surely the hon. member would not suggest that human lives are not valuable. We assess them at a high rate, because the

The Address-Mr. Quelch more manpower you have, the greater potential productive power there is in the country. Therefore we should look upon every human being as a great asset. Our main complaint has been that in the past we have regarded the people of a country as a liability, and have deplored the fact that we have unemployment instead of rejoicing in the fact that we have surplus productive capacity to make it possible to increase the production of the country, improve the standard of living of the people and at the same time reduce the hours of labour. Certainly we would be the last ones to look upon the people as a liability rather than an asset.
There is just one other point I want to deal with at this stage. The hon. member referred to profits and insinuated that it was wrong to produce for profit. I think that people will be obliged to agree, whether they believe in profits or not, that they are a great incentive to production. I claim that everybody who works, either with his brain or with his hands, works for a profit, whether it be a labourer or whether it be what some like to call a capitalist. It is true that when the labourer works he should take an interest in the type of work he does, but he hopes to profit by his work and therefore he will always try to get the highest wage possible in order to profit more. On the other hand, that does not mean for one minute that we condone exorbitant profits or excess profits. But those are things that can well be taken care of by taxation.
By the just price.

When the hon. member for Vancouver East was speaking, he disagreed with us in our argument that in normal times there is invariably a deficiency of purchasing power with which to buy the produced consumer goods of a country. Instead of dealing with that matter at this moment, I will deal with it later on when I shall be dealing with a situation which developed in this country during certain years.
After being in this house for the past fourteen years, I want to say that I am more convinced than ever that the people of this country will never reach the objective towards which they are striving until the principles of social credit are adopted in some form or other either by this government or by some other government.
Both nationally and internationally.

Furthermore, I would say that either the principles of social credit will be adopted or private enterprise will go, and in its place will come some form of "ism" which we may not like but which, once we have 
had it, we may have a great deal of difficulty in getting rid of. It is only necessary to refer to what has happened in the past fifteen years in certain parts of Europe to appreciate what I am referring to. We maintain that by the adoption of social credit principles it will be possible at all times to maintain the optimum development of the resources of the country in order to give the people of Canada the highest standard of living that the country is capable of producing, at the same time giving them the greatest degree of personal freedom possible. In order that a high standard of living may be maintained, we have always advocated that it would be necessary to use a certain amount of national money for the purpose of maintaining the purchasing power of the people at a level sufficiently high to maintain an effective demand against the production of the country. We have never advocated that more money should be issued than was necessary to maintain an effective demand. In other words, we are advocating that national money shall be issued to equate demand with supply.
We have always said that.

It must be quite obvious that this is essential if we are to maintain the full development of our resources, because just the minute that demand lags behind supply, industry will reduce production, since no industry can continue to produce unless it can sell.
It is true that most political parties would say that they believe in maintaining the full development of our resources; but the other three parties, the Liberals, the Conservatives and the C.C.F., advocate that it be done out of taxation or by borrowing. When you borrow money you increase debt. When you increase debt, you increase debt charges. When you increase debt charges, you have to increase taxation in order to pay them, and when you increase taxation you reduce the purchasing power of the people and thereby make it impossible to maintain an effective demand, resulting in unemployment, and then you are on your way into the spiral of a depression.
When the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) introduced the budget last year, he told us that we had a new high in production, in employment and in prosperity. Already this session we have heard words to that effect. But the Minister of Finance went on to warn us that we could not expect that situation to continue indefinitely into the future. As a matter of fact, he warned us that there might be a recession in the not distant future. Therefore, in view of the fact that we have

a large national debt, the government considered it a wise policy to tax the people heavily while they had the money because, the minister said, if a recession comes they will not have so much money. Therefore the only thing to do was for the government to tax the money while they had it. It will be recalled that during the past two years the government have taxed from the people $1,200 million more than was required to meet government expenditures, and the national debt was reduced to quite an extent. But here is the point. The minister emphasized the fact that we had a high level of income, production and employment. Then he warned us that a recession might come, but instead of trying to safeguard the country against a depression developing he instituted a policy which hastened the day of the depression, because he maintained taxation at a high level, thereby withdrawing from circulation $1,200 million, and thereby of course reducing the purchasing power of the people to that extent.
When the minister told us that we had a new high in production, in employment and prosperity, I think he might also have reminded the house that we had, and still have, a new high in discontent; discontent among the workers, discontent among the farmers. You can find it wherever you go. Not only is there discontent among the workers but there is a high degree of fear in the minds of all people, fear as to what is going to happen in the future, fear as to whether or not there will be a depression. Why does that situation exist at a time when we are supposed to have such a high degree of prosperity? I think it is easy to understand why that situation exists. It exists because the people can remember only too clearly what happened in this country during the past nineteen or twenty years. They remember the nine years of the depression when many people lost their life savings, and in some cases their health and in other cases even their lives. They remember the five years of war and the various restrictions that were placed upon their movement. I suppose there is hardly a family in Canada that did not suffer the loss of a relative or a friend. They remember only too well the last four years of high prices and the inflationary period. There is no doubt that many people have prospered during that period, but on the other hand there are many people who have suffered, and suffered severely. I have in mind the people in the low-income brackets, and especially those on low fixed incomes, such as old age pensions, and those on the war veterans allowances. At last they are hoping that we may be approaching an era where there might be a fairly high

But instead of being able to look forward to an era of prosperity, they are now being warned on every side that the danger is that we are going into another depression. Therefore, is it any wonder that fear is expressed on all sides today and that there is widespread discontent? I believe all hon. members will agree that it is a somewhat dreary outlook. People are asking the question whether or not depressions are inevitable. Just because people in other parts of the world suffer depressions, is it any reason why we in this country have to have one? I am not suggesting for one minute, Mr. Speaker, that the problem is an easy one to solve; but I do suggest that the situation has been greatly aggravated by various blunders on the part of the government, blunders which will always occur so long as the government ties itself to an orthodox financial system. We believe that these difficulties could have been avoided under a system of social credit. Let me give an example of what I mean when I say that. Let me deal briefly with the three periods that I have mentioned, namely, the depression years, in the thirties, the war years and the postwar years.
Yesterday the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) referred to the depression years from 1930 to 1935. Let me go on from there and deal with the years from 1935 to 1939. What was the situation in Canada at that time? During that period we had around a million people on relief, half a million people unemployed, and industry operating at less than 50 per cent of its capacity. In addition, strangely enough, during those five years we had, on an average, a favourable balance of payments of over $219 million. In other words, we had exported $219 million worth of goods more than we brought back in imports. During those years it was a very common thing for people to blame industry for the situation. They asked, why does not industry have more confidence? Why does not industry employ more of the unemployed, expand its production and produce the things that the people require? I think the answer to that question is quite obvious. Industrial production at that time was less than 50 per cent of its capacity. Even with that low production, industry was having a great deal of difficulty in selling that limited production. Industry knew only too well that

The Address-Mr. Quelch if they expanded their production they would just have that much more goods left unsold and they would go bankrupt that much quicker. It was in those years that the social credit movement originated in Alberta. It is interesting to note that after fourteen years the Social Credit government of Alberta was returned stronger than ever.
What was the analysis we made at that time, an analysis which is just as sound today as it was then? Fortunately more and more people are coming to realize the soundness of that analysis. At that time we said that owing to certain practices inherent in the capitalistic system industry was not able to distribute sufficient purchasing power in the form of wages, salaries and dividends to maintain an effective demand against its own production except-and here is the point that most people ignore-in times of abnormal capital goods construction, such as you have in wartime, or in the early development years of a country. And the reason of course that purchasing power at that time can increase to the point necessary to maintain effective demand against the production of the country is that the money paid out in the construction of roads, bridges and the like is not required to buy those roads and bridges. Therefore that money becomes available to buy the consumer goods upon the market. Therefore, the higher the degree of capital construction in relation to production of consumer goods, the more purchasing power will there be in circulation for the purpose of maintaining an effective demand against the production of consumer goods in the country.
It was that point to which the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) took exception. He said that in his opinion industry always distributed sufficient moneys in salaries, wages and dividends to buy back this production. I pointed out that owing to certain practices inherent within the system, that was not so.
Let me give an example. In the first place, banks create money and lend it, but they do not create the money to pay the interest on the loan. They charge interest on the money they lend. But they do not provide the money for which the interest is paid.
A deficiency is created, therefore, to the extent that total interest paid exceeds wages and dividends paid out by banks. Then take, for example, an industry which produces $10,000 worth of goods. We will say that in the production of those goods the industry pays out $10,000. Therefore you have $10,000 available to buy back $10,000 worth of goods. But if $1,000 of that $10,000 is saved, then only $9,000 is available to buy the $10,000 v-orth of goods, and you have a deficiency


of $1,000. As we know, people are being continuously urged and advised to save more money. The more you save, the greater that deficiency will become, unless other steps are taken to make up the deficiency in purchasing power existing as a result of the saving.
Then again, the industry will have certain profits. If the people benefiting from those profits proceed to spend them, there is no deficiency in purchasing power. But we all know that many industries make a practice of not distributing all their profits. They plough them back. To the extent the profits are not distributed, you will have a deficiency.
Those are three simple examples of how a deficiency of purchasing power occurs. I do not wish to go into it in greater detail now. Rather than argue the point further I believe it would be better to give one or two concrete examples to prove that in the past the purchasing power of the people has not been sufficient to buy the total production of the country. Let us see what happened in England for two hundred years prior to 1914. Let me quote what was said by Reginald McKenna to the American Bankers Association on October 5, 1922. These are his words:
For over two centuries British capital, that is, credit, has been lent to other countries: year by year England produced more than she either consumed herself or could exchange for the products of other nations, and she could not obtain a market for the surplus unless she gave the purchaser a long credit. Foreign loans and foreign issues were taken up in England and the proceeds were spent in paying for the surplus production. British factories and workshops were kept in good employment,-
And this is the important point-
-but it was a condition of their prosperity that a part of their output should be disposed of in this way.
In other words, during those years of production industry found it impossible to sell its total output within England, or the imports brought back in return. In order to maintain production it was necessary to ship surplus goods out of the country, and to refuse to accept imports in return. So that the money paid out in the production which was exported, and for which no goods were brought back in return, helped to maintain an effective demand against the goods left within the country.
That is why one will find all great industrial nations have insisted in the past-as they still do-upon trying to maintain a favourable balance of trade in order to prevent unemployment. That is one of the main reasons we took such strong exception to the Bretton Woods agreement; because under the Bretton Woods agreement we find the great industrial nations endeavouring to maintain

a favourable balance of trade merely for the purpose of dumping their own unemployment problem upon the doorstep of another nation.
Let me quote from a survey made in the United States under the direction of the government of that country. In 1934 the Hoover administration set up a committee of technicians to make a national survey of the potential productive capacity of the United States. Let me quote from the foreword to that book:
After almost a year of research by sixty technicians, financed by the federal government, the national survey of potential product capacity has released its findings. Official publication will follow in due course. Preliminary thereto, Mr. Loeb, the director of the survey, here describes the results.
Let me quote two short paragraphs from this survey, one which is well worth reading because it illustrates much better than I can do the manner in which a deficiency of purchasing power has curtailed production. At page 71 I find this:
The total national monetary income in 1929 did not equal the total price asked for the goods which could have been produced by the plant then existing. But instead of dropping prices until monetary income was able to command full production (which is the classical answer to this situation), prices were maintained and production was restricted. Consequently, national monetary income did not in 1929, nor does it today, command the full production of our industrial plant.
Then, later in the book, they make certain suggestions. Perhaps I did not mention the name of this book; it is "The Chart of Plenty". One of the conclusions at page 161 states:
It would seem that the simple and obvious way out, that of giving a buying power adequate to procure desired goods and services to the limit of our ability to produce them, might well be tried. It is simple in principle but has not been attempted.
That is social credit.

And that is what we maintain. There you have sixty technicians appointed by the government of the United States to make a survey - of the potential capacity of that country; and they bring in a report which states that the logical way to deal with the situation is to issue money to maintain the purchasing power of the people to a point where the people will be able to buy the total production of the country.
Let me return to the point I was making earlier. I was stating that during the year of depression we had a situation wherein our production was less than 50 per cent of its capacity. We were not able to expand our production, because the people did not have money to buy even the reduced supply of goods then being produced. Industry knew only too well that if they expanded their production they would have that much more goods left unsold. So in those years we .	29087-89

The Prime Minister's answer was as follows:
The answer to the first part of the question is yes. The answer to the second part of the question is that the brief is still under consideration.
That last line sounds rather familiar. If that answer had been given by one of the Prime Minister's lesser colleagues I might have termed it as being glib, but having an appreciation of the sincerity of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) I shall merely say that the answer was brief. But in any case it was not satisfactory.
My purpose in rising is to place on the record the details of this brief so that members of the house and people outside the house may be informed. I sometimes think that it takes a brave man to bring up the subject of education on the floor of this house. When one does venture upon that particular subject he is told immediately that it has to do solely with the provinces. As we have reason to know, this session there are those who are very zealous of provincial rights.

I offer no excuse for bringing up the matter of education on the floor of this or any other house. To me education is fundamental. I shall be very brief with the philosophical part of my discourse, if I may call it that. Education is our hope for democracy.
I would say that it is our only hope for unity, both national and international. It is our hope for physical survival itself. If enlightenment does not secure national and international unity, then I do not think there is any other agency that will secure it.
During times of crisis, . and particularly during times of war, there are those who say that education can wait. Education is the first casualty of war. The thing to do in a case of that kind as a substitute for education is to accumulate gadgets. The accumulation of gadgets, by the way, seems to be one of the main hobbies of the people of the North American continent. In times of war we substitute for real education large doses of scientific knowledge which enable us to perform certain functions which have to do with the process of war but which, after the war is over, leave the mind perfectly barren as far as general education is concerned. And scientific knowledge of itself is not enough.
I know it has been scientifically proven that acquired characteristics cannot be handed down to another generation by means of heredity. That is why education must be a continuing process, because we can get no knowledge from our parents through the processes of heredity. What I mean to say is that a generation or two generations cannot neglect education and then expect to resume where they left off. Similarly, in the case of democracy it has to be worked at to be retained, and it has to be passed on not by heredity but rather by precept and example. In that sense education to me is like freedom of speech. Irrespective of the conditions under which I live, as long as I can retain it I can use it to obtain ultimate justice; but, if I lose it, it is in a measure like losing my own soul.
Culture can be lost. A generation can be left in darkness. Remember, that generation which is left in darkness does not come back of its own volition and demand the light. It does not know enough to do that. That is the reason why certain conditions in some European countries today are a cause for real alarm because, given a generation or two of darkness, these people will have to start the long slow process of education again. As I said before, it can only be done by a continuing process.

What I have to say will take only about two minutes, Mr. Speaker. It concerns a matter which it would be difficult to discuss on a question of privilege; therefore I am taking this opportunity of bringing it to the attention of the house and the country.
On March 1 the broadcasting station at Moose Jaw, CHAB, carried a news report in which Mr. Sam Carr was referred to as a "Ukrainian-born former organizer of the Canadian communist party." In view of the serious charges that have been made against Mr. Carr, which call in question his loyalty to this country, it is important that no wrong impressions should be created by inaccurate news items such as the one to which I have referred.
When this newscast was brought to my attention by a resident of the province of Saskatchewan I immediately went to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) who, after checking with the commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, confirmed my belief that Mr. Carr was neither of Ukrainian nationality nor of Ukrainian racial descent. I want to make it clear that I am not interested in what Mr. Carr's nationality or racial origin may be, but I am interested in clearing up any misunderstanding or wrong impression that may have been created by this erroneous newscast.
Canadians of Ukrainian origin wish to completely dissociate themselves from any such activities as those with which Mr. Carr has been charged. Their loyalty to Canada is beyond question, and they wish to keep it so. More than forty thousand Ukrainians, that is Canadians of Ukrainian origin, served in the armed forces of Canada in world war II. Many of them made the supreme sacrifice. Those who remained at home sought to promote Canada's war effort in every way possible, and have a fine record of voluntary service in such organizations as the Canadian Red Cross, Canadian victory clubs

and various other organizations which in time of need serve the nation on a voluntary basis. It is therefore understandable that such an erroneous news report as the one to which I have referred would create resentment and bring forth protests from our peace-loving and law-abiding citizens. I am informed by the manager of the radio station at Moose Jaw that the news item in question came from the British United Press. Accordingly I have communicated with the manager of that news service, asking him to have an appropriate correction made.
I am making this statement in the house today in order to clear up any misunderstanding or wrong impression which may have been created by the news report broadcast by the Moose Jaw radio station on March 1, by placing formally on the record the correct position with regard to this matter.

To indicate the sort of thing I have in mind I want to refer briefly to what I think is a serious charge against the pension officials. I have before me the case of a young man of this province who served in His Majesty's forces from June of 1942 to October of 1945. He was in the naval service and was on some particularly dangerous missions in the course of which, from the evidence as I gather it, he suffered a form of battle fatigue. The young man came back to this country, married and now has two children, a fairly good position, and is buying his own home. Because of his mental state he went to the authorities in Hamilton in January of 1946, within three months of his discharge from the service. At that time the examining doctor was of the opinion, as I have it here in a letter from the director general of treatment services, that no treatment was required. After being told by the officials in Hamilton and those at Christie Street hospital, to which he went later, that treatment was not necessary in his case, being concerned about his mental state he went to a private doctor in Hamilton and, according to the evidence furnished the pension board, started treatment at his own expense within the year of his free entitlement, that is in July of 1946.
I have in my hand receipts covering medical treatment by the psychiatrist, Dr. Finlayson, and other Hamilton doctors, which this young man received as a result of trying to look after his own case because the Department of Veterans Affairs did not consider his case sufficiently serious to recommend D.V.A. treatment.
The medical bills that I have here, running throughout the last year and a half or two years, in the aggregate amount to well over $500. This man was advised to apply for a pension. In a letter to me he said he did not want a pension. All he wanted was his hospital bills paid and the opportunity to return for free treatment for his mental condition. His bills have been turned down. He has been refused the right of treatment.
This man may not have a case, but I feel that he has. I have talked to him. I find him to be a fine young man. The pension board speaks of his straightforward and frank manner in giving evidence before the board. He may be frank, he may be straightforward, he may be everything; but the fact is that he was still turned down, and he is

The Address-Division paying from $25 to $50 a month for his own medical treatment. That is not good enough from a country which he served as he did. Every member of this house has similar cases.
Before I take my seat I want to plead with other hon. members and with the cabinet to make certain that the so-called bureaucrats -I do not like to speak in disparaging terms of the officers in charge of any government department; I know they have a job to do- carry out government policies. It is time that the ministers of the government made certain that the policies they talk about on the hustings are enforced by the employees of the government itself.
